| [THEORY-067](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-067.md) | Self-control over time needs no faculty of will: interests that dominate at different delays bargain, and resolve is the recursive staking of expected future choices on the present one | Ainslie's précis ([LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md)): hyperbolic discounting makes a smaller, sooner reward temporarily preferred, so successive "interests" conflict as in a repeated prisoner's dilemma. Treating a choice as a precedent bundles the series, and summed hyperbolic curves favour the larger, later rewards; a lapse costs credibility. Will is that recursion, not an organ. Schelling ([LIT-602](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-602.md)) describes the same divided chooser from the side of tactics: we manage our later selves as we manage other people. The mathematics of bundling is sound; that willpower works this way is argued, and the précis concedes it is hard to test directly. It is a claim about how control is achieved, not about whose control is self-governance. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-149](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-149.md) | Users can govern a shared resource durably without either privatisation or central control, and the institutions that last are marked not by particular rules but by structural regularities: user-made and user-monitored rules, graduated sanctions, cheap local conflict resolution, recognised rights to self-organise, and nested layers of governance | Ostrom's account, read in her Nobel lecture ([LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md)). Coded case meta-analyses, laboratory and field experiments and multi-country field studies agree that resource users often self-govern successfully. Long-surviving institutions share eight design principles that failed ones lack. The principles are correlates of survival, not tested causes, and their reach beyond common-pool resources is not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-290](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-290.md) v2 | In a two-debater, three-proposition model of deductive debate whose payoff trades true beliefs against changes of mind, the most truth-conducive equilibrium can fall short of the truth-optimal profile because one debater free-rides on the other's belief-disrupting arguments, and in a narrow band of mixed equilibria a higher weight on truth gives lower equilibrium accuracy | Handfield, Garcia, Hilbe and Yeo (2025), [LIT-966](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-966.md), read in full in [NOTE-795](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-795.md). With payoff w·v − d (true beliefs against changes of mind), debate between two deductive reasoners is a cooperative dilemma at low and moderate truth weights. Typically one argues boldly and the other free-rides (a snowdrift), and at low weights both exit. A small dip in accuracy as w rises occurs in a narrow band of mixed equilibria. It is shown numerically for two players and three propositions. It concerns collective accuracy, not a belief the pair settles on, and at high truth weight in short debates there is no dilemma. The title claims the model only; groups and richer strategies are QUESTION-173. | Active |
| [THEORY-404](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-404.md) | With a common prior, a sender who commits to a signal the receiver observes can induce any distribution of posteriors whose mean is the prior, so an openly designed experiment moves a fully informed Bayesian receiver whenever the concave closure of the sender's value lies above its value at the prior; at the optimum, under the paper's tie-breaking, the receiver is certain when she takes the sender's worst action and indifferent when she takes another | Kamenica & Gentzkow (2011), [LIT-1021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1021.md), read in [NOTE-717](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-717.md) with the proofs. Proved results (Proposition 1, Corollary 2, Propositions 4 and 5) for a single ideal Bayesian receiver, a finite state space, commitment and sender-preferred tie-breaking. A judge who knows the investigation was designed to convict convicts 60 percent of defendants when 70 percent are innocent. The paper does not analyse manipulation, does not compute the receiver's welfare and does not cite Blackwell. | Active |
| [THEORY-414](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-414.md) | Institutions are rules in equilibrium, correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria that the players represent to themselves as rules, and a constitutive rule 'X counts as Y in C' is a regulative rule split by a coined term into a base rule and a status rule, so the term adds a name and cognitive economy but no new kind of fact | Hindriks & Guala (2015, online 2014), [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md), read with the authors' reply to six commentators in [NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md). The equilibrium half is a clear synthesis of Lewis, Aumann, Aoki and Greif. The reduction of Searle's constitutive rules is worked once, for a toy first-occupancy property, and asserted in general; it depends on a reading of "collective acceptance" loose enough to make the "counts as" biconditionals hold by construction, and on extensional equivalence of behaviour. The reply adds that a right is a bundle of others' regulative obligations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-437](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-437.md) | When each agent's feasible actions depend on the others' actions, an equilibrium exists if every action set is a contractible polyhedron, every constraint correspondence has a closed graph with non-empty compact values, payoffs and the maximum-value functions are continuous, and every best-response set is contractible; convexity is not needed | Debreu (1952), [LIT-067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-067.md), read in full in [NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md). The theorem (p. 888) is proved by applying the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product of best-response correspondences. A Remark reduces the continuity of the value function to a compact graph plus continuity (lower hemicontinuity) of the constraint. It is existence only, in finite dimensions with finitely many agents and real-valued payoffs. That it contains Nash's theorem is asserted; the reduction is routine but not in the paper. | Active |
| [THEORY-457](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-457.md) | When people can choose their cooperation partners and have equal outside options, the stable division of jointly produced gains is in proportion to each partner's contribution, and partner choice selects for a genuine sense of fairness as proportionality | Baumard, André & Sperber (2013), [LIT-508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-508.md), read in [NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md), with its 28 commentaries and Response. The pairwise result is cited from another paper; the extension to effort and talent is unproven by the authors' own statement. The evidence is a reinterpretation of dictator, ultimatum, trust and public-goods results as allocation by entitlement. The authors disagree among themselves about whether purity, loyalty and kin care are moral at all. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-466](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-466.md) | Among contestants of equal prowess with dangerous weapons, individual selection can favour conventional fighting backed by retaliation: an escalating Hawk is not evolutionarily stable, Retaliator is at most neutrally stable because Mouse ties it, and in a contest settled by persistence alone no fixed persistence is stable while an exponential mixture is | Maynard Smith & Price (1973), [LIT-505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-505.md), read in full in [NOTE-404](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-404.md). A simulation of five strategies, 2,000 contests per pairing, shows that "limited war" can be favoured by individual selection, without benefit to the species. The paper calls Retaliator an ESS "though Mouse does equally well", which fails its own second condition. There is no Hawk–Dove game, no "dove", no difference in prowess and no ownership, so it is not the source of display, deference or owner–intruder conventions. | Active |
| [THEORY-468](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-468.md) | Morality is the set of solutions to recurrent problems of cooperation, so each of the seven cooperation problems game theory identifies yields a moral domain valued in every culture, and behaviour unrelated to cooperation is morally neutral | Curry (2016), [LIT-503](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-503.md), read in [NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md), with its two tests, [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md) ([NOTE-034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-034.md)) and [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md) ([NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md)). The positive half has support: the seven are described as good wherever ethnographers record them, and questionnaire items for them form seven factors. The negative half, that nothing else is moralized, is the theory's own stated prediction (p. 40). No study in the programme has tested it blind, and where non-cooperative items appear, the programme's own data show them moralized. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-567](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-567.md) | In the donation game, where a cooperator pays c for another to get b, defectors win in a well-mixed population, and each of five mechanisms makes cooperators evolutionarily stable above a benefit-to-cost threshold: kin selection r > c/b, direct reciprocity w > c/b, indirect reciprocity q > c/b, network reciprocity b/c > k and group selection b/c > 1 + n/m; the rules cover altruism only, not mutualism, coordination or conflict | Nowak (2006), [LIT-501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-501.md), read in [NOTE-409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-409.md), main text only. A four-page review that casts each known mechanism as a 2×2 game so that one set of criteria applies to all. The five ESS conditions are confirmed by the main text; the derivations are in the supporting material, which was not read, and in cited papers. Several rules hold only under weak selection, regular graphs or rare group splitting. Every mechanism is modelled with the donation game, so mutualism, coordination and conflict are outside it. | Active |
| [THEORY-672](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-672.md) | In the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with a probability w of meeting again, no strategy does better against an established TIT FOR TAT than TIT FOR TAT does against itself if and only if w ≥ (T−R)/(T−P) and w ≥ (T−R)/(R−S); always defecting is stable for every w, a cluster of reciprocators can invade it, and a nice stable strategy resists clusters, but the stability is only neutral, since always cooperating ties | Axelrod & Hamilton (1981), [LIT-498](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-498.md), read in full in [NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md). Against TIT FOR TAT the best reply is always-defect or alternation, which gives the condition on w. The cluster result and the "ratchet" are explicit payoff comparisons. "Evolutionarily stable" here means no mutant does better, which is weaker than Maynard Smith and Price's definition: always cooperate does exactly as well. The model is deterministic and error-free. Tournament robustness is a separate, empirical claim about the strategies people submitted. | Active |
